pharm: Gastric acid neutralizer combined with GI antispasmodic for symptomatic dyspepsia and abdominal cramp relief
quick: 1-2 tablets/10-15 mL after meals & at bedtime; varies by brand
Take 1-3 h after meals and at bedtime for best effect
Avoid antispasmodic; use simple antacid if needed
Caution; anticholinergics may reduce milk and pass into milk
Limit; worsens dyspepsia and adds sedation
Symptom relief, bowel habit; electrolytes if prolonged
summary: A fixed-dose combination pairing one or more antacids (e.g. aluminium hydroxide, magnesium hydroxide/trisilicate, magaldrate) with an antispasmodic (commonly the anticholinergic dicyclomine or oxyphenonium, sometimes with simethicone) for symptomatic relief of acid dyspepsia, hyperacidity, gastritis and accompanying abdominal cramps/colic. The antacid neutralizes gastric acid while the antispasmodic relaxes GI smooth muscle. Composition and doses vary widely by brand - this is an OTC/group product, not a single FDA-approved formulation; anticholinergic cautions (glaucoma, urinary retention, ileus) and antacid drug-absorption interactions apply.
indications: Symptomatic relief of hyperacidity, acid dyspepsia and heartburn accompanied by abdominal cramps or spasm
Gastritis and non-ulcer dyspepsia with colicky abdominal pain
Functional GI spasm/flatulent dyspepsia (simethicone-containing variants for trapped gas)

dosage.d: 1-2 tablets chewed/swallowed after meals and at bedtime
dosage.n: Exact strength varies by brand - follow product label

dosage.d: 10-15 mL after meals and at bedtime
dosage.n: Shake well; antacid component dictates volume

dosage.d: Use for limited duration (a few days); reassess if symptoms persist
dosage.n: Do not exceed maximum stated on label

dosage.d: Use lowest effective dose; prefer brands without anticholinergic
Avoid combination products unless specifically directed by a clinician

admin: Take 1-3 hours after meals and at bedtime when symptoms are typically worst
Chew chewable tablets thoroughly; shake suspensions well before measuring
Separate from other oral drugs by at least 2 hours (antacid reduces their absorption)
Use for short-term symptomatic relief only; seek review if symptoms persist beyond a few days
Do not exceed the maximum daily dose stated on the specific product label
moa: Dual mechanism. The antacid component (aluminium hydroxide, magnesium hydroxide/trisilicate, magaldrate or combinations) chemically neutralizes hydrochloric acid in the stomach, raising intragastric pH and reducing pepsin activity; magnesium salts tend to be laxative while aluminium salts are constipating, so they are combined to balance bowel effects. The antispasmodic component relieves abdominal cramp - anticholinergics (e.g. dicyclomine, oxyphenonium) block muscarinic receptors to reduce GI smooth-muscle tone and motility, while dicyclomine also has a direct smooth-muscle relaxant action; simethicone-containing variants reduce surface tension of gas bubbles to relieve bloating.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to any antacid or antispasmodic component
Urinary retention / obstructive uropathy or significant BPH - anticholinergic
Paralytic ileus, GI obstruction, severe/toxic ulcerative colitis or megacolon - anticholinergic
Infants and breastfeeding mothers (for dicyclomine-containing products)
relative: Cardiac disease/tachyarrhythmia, reflux esophagitis (anticholinergic lowers LES tone)
monitor: Bowel habit (constipation from aluminium/anticholinergic vs diarrhea from magnesium)
Anticholinergic effects - dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary hesitancy
Persistence of symptoms suggesting need for diagnostic work-up

preg: The antacid components are generally considered acceptable for short-term symptomatic use in pregnancy (avoid high-dose/long-term sodium-containing antacids). The antispasmodic/anticholinergic component (e.g. dicyclomine) is best avoided in pregnancy unless clearly needed; prefer a plain antacid. Follow the specific product label and clinician advice.
lact: Antacids are poorly absorbed and generally compatible with breastfeeding. Anticholinergic antispasmodics (notably dicyclomine) can pass into breast milk and may reduce milk supply; dicyclomine is contraindicated in breastfeeding infants. Prefer a plain antacid while nursing.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment. Magnesium salts can accumulate causing hypermagnesemia, and aluminium can accumulate causing toxicity (including in dialysis patients); aluminium-containing antacids may also bind phosphate. Avoid prolonged or high-dose use and consider lower doses with monitoring.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is generally required for the antacid component. Use the anticholinergic component cautiously, as reduced GI motility and anticholinergic effects may be less well tolerated in advanced liver disease.

major: Tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones - antacid chelation markedly reduces absorption; separate by >=2-4 h
Other anticholinergics/antimuscarinics - additive toxicity (dry mouth, retention, confusion, ileus)
moderate: Iron salts, levothyroxine, bisphosphonates, azole antifungals (ketoconazole/itraconazole), atazanavir - reduced absorption by antacid; separate dosing
Digoxin, phenytoin, gabapentin, mycophenolate - lowered absorption/levels
Enteric-coated drugs - raised gastric pH can cause premature dissolution
minor: Salicylates - urinary alkalinization (sodium/Mg antacids) can increase excretion
H2 blockers/PPIs - additive acid reduction (usually intended)
interactions.food: Take after meals; the antacid is most effective 1-3 h post-meal. Avoid taking with other oral medicines or food that contains divalent cations at the same time.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol - it aggravates dyspepsia/gastritis and may add to anticholinergic drowsiness.
interactions.diagnostics: Antacids can raise gastric/urinary pH; magnesium/aluminium antacids may alter serum electrolytes and phosphate. Anticholinergics may interfere with gastric secretion or motility studies.

serious: Hypermagnesemia or aluminium toxicity in renal impairment
rare: Milk-alkali syndrome with excessive calcium-containing antacid use
emergency: Acute angle-closure glaucoma (severe eye pain, vision loss, headache)
Severe anticholinergic toxicity (hyperthermia, delirium, seizures) - usually overdose

monitoring: Symptom response (acid symptoms and cramp relief)
Bowel habit - balance of constipation vs diarrhea
Anticholinergic adverse effects, particularly in the elderly
Serum magnesium, aluminium and electrolytes if used long-term or in renal impairment
counsel: Take after meals and at bedtime; chew chewable tablets well
Do not take other medicines, iron or antibiotics at the same time - separate by at least 2 hours
Expect possible dry mouth, blurred vision or constipation from the antispasmodic
Use short-term only; see a doctor if symptoms last more than a few days, or with weight loss, vomiting, black stools or trouble swallowing
Tell your doctor if you have glaucoma, prostate/urinary problems, heart disease or kidney disease before using
pk: Antacid acid neutralization within minutes; antispasmodic relief ~1-2 h
Antacid effect peaks ~30 min; dicyclomine plasma peak ~1-1.5 h
Dicyclomine ~1.8 h (terminal ~9-10 h); antacids act locally, minimally absorbed
Antacid 20-60 min on empty stomach, up to ~3 h with food; antispasmodic ~4 h
Store at room temperature (20-25 C); keep suspensions tightly closed, do not freeze
pearls: This is a combination drug GROUP / OTC product, not a single FDA-approved product - exact composition and doses vary by brand, so clinicians should always check the specific product label
Magnesium salts are laxative and aluminium salts are constipating - they are combined to balance bowel effects
Antacids reduce absorption of many drugs (tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, iron, levothyroxine, bisphosphonates) - separate dosing by at least 2 hours
Avoid the anticholinergic component in glaucoma, urinary retention/BPH, paralytic ileus, severe ulcerative colitis and myasthenia gravis
Use cautiously in renal impairment (magnesium/aluminium accumulation) and in the elderly (anticholinergic confusion, retention)
Persistent or alarm symptoms (weight loss, dysphagia, GI bleeding) warrant investigation, not continued symptomatic use
missed: These products are usually taken as needed for symptoms rather than on a fixed schedule. If on a regular schedule, take the missed dose when remembered; skip it if the next dose is near. Do not double up.
overdose: Antacid overdose may cause diarrhea (magnesium), constipation (aluminium), electrolyte disturbance and, in renal impairment, hypermagnesemia or aluminium toxicity. Antispasmodic (anticholinergic) overdose causes dry flushed skin, dilated pupils, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, agitation, hyperthermia, delirium and seizures. Treatment is supportive; physostigmine may be considered for severe central anticholinergic toxicity. Seek emergency care for large ingestions.
